pages.text: Right now, as you read this page, your heart is beating. It has been beating since before you were born, starting around three weeks after conception and continuing, without pause, for every second of your life. By the time you reach the age of 70, your heart will have beaten approximately two and a half billion times. It will never once have stopped to rest.

image.note: Illustration: anatomically accurate human heart with major vessels labelled

pages.text: The heart is a muscle, roughly the size of your fist, located in the centre of your chest, slightly to the left. Its job is to pump blood around the body. It does this by contracting and relaxing rhythmically: squeezing blood out with each contraction, filling with blood again with each relaxation. This squeezing and filling is what you feel as your heartbeat.

An adult human heart beats between 60 and 100 times per minute at rest. During intense exercise, it can beat more than 200 times per minute. A newborn baby's heart beats between 120 and 160 times per minute. The hearts of smaller, faster animals beat much more quickly: a mouse's heart beats around 600 times per minute. The heart of a blue whale, the largest animal on earth, beats only four to eight times per minute.

Blood does not simply slosh about; it travels a precise circuit mapped four hundred years ago by the English doctor William Harvey. Before him, physicians believed the liver constantly made new blood that the body used up. Harvey proved, by careful measurement, that the same blood circulates round and round, pushed by the heart. It was one of medicine's greatest discoveries, and it was ridiculed at first. Careful evidence, in the end, won.

The heart has four chambers: two upper chambers called atria and two lower chambers called ventricles. The right side of the heart receives oxygen-depleted blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs. The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Both sides work simultaneously, contracting in a coordinated rhythm governed by electrical signals.

image.note: Diagram of the four-chambered heart showing blood flow direction through right and left sides with arrows

pages.text: The valves of the heart are one-way gates that ensure blood flows in the correct direction. There are four valves. They open and close with each heartbeat. The sound of the valves closing is the sound doctors listen for with a stethoscope: the lub-dub that is the heartbeat. If a valve is damaged or malformed, blood can flow in the wrong direction, a condition called a heart murmur, which varies in seriousness from negligible to life-threatening.

The heart's electrical system is one of the most remarkable things in biology. A group of cells in the upper right atrium, called the sinoatrial node, generates electrical signals at a steady rate. These signals travel through the heart along a specialised conducting system, triggering the muscle cells to contract in the correct sequence. The sinoatrial node is the heart's natural pacemaker. An artificial pacemaker, a small device implanted under the skin, can take over this function when the natural one fails.

The heart pumps blood through two separate circulations that work simultaneously. Pulmonary circulation carries blood from the heart to the lungs and back. In the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. Systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood from the heart to every organ and tissue in the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients and collecting waste products.

Stretched end to end, the blood vessels of one human body would circle the earth twice: about a hundred thousand kilometres of arteries, veins, and tiny capillaries. The capillaries are the point of it all. So narrow that blood cells pass in single file, their walls are thin enough for oxygen and nutrients to slip through to every living cell, and for waste to slip back. The mighty heart exists to serve these microscopic threads.

Blood itself is a busy crowd. Red cells, shaped like tiny cushions, carry oxygen using iron-rich haemoglobin, which is what makes blood red. White cells hunt invaders as a mobile army. Platelets rush to seal any leak, forming clots that stop bleeding. Floating plasma carries them all, along with food, hormones, and heat. A single drop of blood contains millions of cells, each with a job, all moving at once.

Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. In Nigeria, cardiovascular disease kills more people than malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV combined. Many of these deaths are preventable. The factors that cause most heart disease are well understood: high blood pressure, high blood cholesterol, smoking, physical inactivity, excess weight, and poorly controlled diabetes.

Regular physical activity is one of the most powerful things a person can do for their heart. Exercise makes the heart muscle stronger. A stronger heart pumps more blood with each beat, which means it needs to beat less frequently to maintain the same circulation. Trained athletes have resting heart rates well below 60 beats per minute because their hearts are so efficient.

pages.text: Food matters too. A diet high in vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, and unsalted nuts is associated with a significantly lower risk of heart disease. Excess salt raises blood pressure. Saturated fat raises blood cholesterol. Processed foods, sweetened drinks, and excess sugar contribute to weight gain, which increases the heart's workload and raises the risk of diabetes.

Blood pressure is the pressure that blood exerts on the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps. High blood pressure, called hypertension, damages artery walls over time and dramatically increases the risk of heart attack and stroke. It often produces no symptoms until serious damage has occurred, which is why it is sometimes called the silent killer. Regular blood pressure checks are a simple, cheap, and effective way of detecting it early.

Some hearts start life with a fault. A hole between chambers, a narrowed valve, a miswired vessel: these congenital heart conditions affect babies in every country. Once, many such children did not survive. Today, surgeons in Nigeria and around the world repair many of these hearts, sometimes on newborns, sometimes before birth. Paediatric heart surgery is among the most demanding work in medicine, and it saves children who would once have been given up as lost.

A heart attack occurs when the blood supply to part of the heart muscle is cut off, usually by a blockage in one of the coronary arteries that supply the heart with its own blood. Without blood, heart muscle cells begin to die within minutes. The longer the blockage lasts, the more damage is done. Recognising the signs and getting treatment quickly saves lives.

The main warning signs of a heart attack are: chest pain or pressure, often described as a heavy weight or tightness; pain spreading to the arm, neck, jaw, or back; shortness of breath; nausea; and sweating. Women sometimes experience different symptoms: unusual fatigue, discomfort in the upper back, and nausea without chest pain. Anyone experiencing these symptoms needs emergency medical attention immediately.

Modern treatment for heart disease has improved dramatically. Coronary bypass surgery, in which blood is rerouted around a blocked artery using a vessel taken from elsewhere in the body, can restore blood flow. Stents, tiny expandable tubes inserted into blocked arteries, can prop them open. Drugs can dissolve clots and prevent new ones from forming. None of these treatments are as good as prevention.

pages.text: The heart that beats in your chest right now is yours to protect. What you eat, how much you move, whether you smoke, and how you manage stress will all influence how well it serves you for the decades ahead. Understanding how the heart works is the first step to making choices that keep it working.

Your heart's future is largely in your hands, starting now. The habits of childhood, what you eat, how much you move, whether you ever take up smoking, set the course for a lifetime. In Nigeria, heart disease is rising fast as cities grow and diets change. The defences are unglamorous and powerful: real food over processed, activity over sitting, no tobacco, and blood-pressure checks in adulthood. Look after the pump that never rests, and it will not let you down.
